question: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Piotr Müller (ECR) Subject:

On 23 March 2026, the Vice-President / High Representative, Kaja Kallas, announced the mobilisation of EUR 66 million in grants and EUR 221 million in low-interest loans for new EU projects in Nigeria, as well as closer cooperation on migration, research and innovation. This decision gives rise to serious misgivings in light of persistent reports of violence against Christians, impunity for perpetrators, and wider violations of human rights and religious freedom in Nigeria. EU financial support must not give the impression that the Union is prepared to turn a blind eye to persecution and poor citizen protection for the sake of maintaining political and migratory cooperation. In light of the above: 1.

What specific conditions pertaining to the protection of human rights, in particular religious freedom and the security of Christian communities, have been tied to the latest EU financial support to Nigeria?
Before this package was announced, was an assessment carried out of the action taken by the Nigerian authorities to prosecute the perpetrators of attacks on Christians and protect civilians?

Does the Vice-President / High Representative intend to make further funding and cooperation with Nigeria contingent on a measurable improvement in the human rights situation and effective action against religious violence?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.6.2026) The Samoa Agreement1, signed between the EU and a number of African, Caribbean and Pacific States including Nigeria, constitutes the overarching legal framework governing, among other matters, the EU-Nigeria cooperation. Article 9 of the Samoa Agreement includes protecting and ensuring the ‘freedom of thought, religion and belief’, thus obliging all signatories not to discriminate based on religion or belief in the exercise and enjoyment of fundamental rights. In addition, under the Samoa Agreement, respect for human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law is an essential element, any breach of which may trigger consultations and, ultimately, appropriate measures, including the suspension of the Agreement or financial transfers. Financial packages under instruments such as Global Gateway are subject to internal programming procedures involving the relevant EU services, as well as strategic alignment with the EU's external action priorities. The EU has consistently expressed its concern about violence affecting all communities in Nigeria, including attacks on both Christian and Muslim communities, and has advocated for accountability and swift responses where such attacks occur. Over the last decade, the EU has invested heavily to support counter-terrorism, stabilisation and rule of law in Nigeria. It is widely recognised that violence in Nigeria is a multifaceted security challenge driven by terrorism, banditry and resource-based intercommunal conflict. It cuts across religious and ethnic lines and affects communities of all faiths. In any case, the EU's cooperation and partnership with Nigeria is not structured around single-issue conditionality.
1Partnership Agreement between the European Union and its Member States, of the one part, and the Members
of the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States, of the other, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/agree_internation/2023/2862/oj.
